lines.text: In less than a hundred years, a people from the grasslands of Mongolia built the largest connected land empire in history.
From Korea... all the way to Eastern Europe.
They had no great cities to start with. No navy. No factories. What they had... was horses.
So the business model was... horses?
Horses, discipline, and one very determined man. I'm Penny, this is Tiny Empires, and this is how the Mongols conquered almost everything.
Picture the Mongolian steppe in the twelfth century. Endless grass, freezing winters, and dozens of rival tribes, constantly raiding each other.
The people here were nomads. They moved with their herds, lived in round felt tents called gers, and learned to ride almost before they could walk.
Around eleven sixty-two, a boy named Temujin was born. When he was still a child, his father was poisoned by Tatar enemies, and his family was abandoned by their own clan.
That is a terrible start.
It was. But Temujin survived, made allies, and won rival after rival. Defeated enemies were not only crushed. Many were absorbed into his own people.
In twelve-oh-six, a great assembly of the tribes proclaimed him Chinggis Khan. In English, we usually say Genghis Khan.
So how did a people of perhaps a million nomads beat empires with tens of millions? Organisation.
The army was built in tens. Ten riders, then a hundred, then a thousand, then ten thousand. Clear, simple, and very easy to command.
Each warrior usually brought several horses, so he could swap to a fresh one and keep riding. A Mongol army could cover distances that seemed impossible to its enemies.
They fought with powerful composite bows, from the saddle. And one of their favourite tricks was the fake retreat.
Wait. Running away was the plan?
Running away was the plan. The enemy chased them... straight into a trap.
Officers were often promoted for ability, not just birth. And the khans later built a network of relay stations, so riders carrying messages could change horses and race across the empire.
The first big target was northern China. The Jin dynasty was rich, powerful, and protected by walls and fortified cities.
Horses are brilliant on open grass. They are less brilliant at climbing city walls.
So the Mongols adapted. They recruited engineers from the lands they conquered, and learned to build siege weapons.
In twelve-fifteen, Zhongdu, the great Jin capital in the north, fell to the Mongols. The Jin emperor had already fled south. Today, its ruins lie inside modern Beijing.
Then the Mongols turned west, to the Khwarazmian Empire, a rich Muslim state in Central Asia and Iran, full of trading cities.
Genghis Khan actually wanted trade. In twelve-eighteen he sent a large merchant caravan.
At the border town of Otrar, the governor had the merchants killed. When Genghis sent envoys to demand justice, the Shah had them killed or humiliated too.
Oh no. That was a mistake.
A huge one. Between twelve-nineteen and twelve twenty-one, the Mongols swept through Bukhara, Samarkand, Merv and other great cities.
Many cities were destroyed, and enormous numbers of people were killed. Medieval chroniclers gave huge figures. Historians argue about the exact numbers, but the destruction was real and terrible.
Genghis Khan died in twelve twenty-seven. But the empire did not fall apart. His sons and grandsons kept expanding it.
His son Ogedei became Great Khan. Under him, Mongol armies pushed deep into Russia, and then into Europe.
In twelve forty-one, they defeated a Polish-led army at Legnica, and a Hungarian army at Mohi, within days of each other.
Is anyone going to stop them?
In twelve forty-two, the armies turned back. One reason often given: Ogedei had died, and the Mongol leaders went home to choose the next Great Khan.
In the Middle East, Genghis Khan's grandson Hulagu marched on Baghdad, one of the greatest cities in the world, and the seat of the Abbasid caliphs.
In twelve fifty-eight, Baghdad was captured and sacked, and the Abbasid caliphate there came to an end.
But even the Mongols had limits. In twelve-sixty, at Ain Jalut, in today's Israel, the Mamluks of Egypt defeated them.
And twice, Mongol fleets sailed for Japan, in twelve seventy-four and twelve eighty-one. Both invasions failed, and storms wrecked much of the second fleet.
Finally! A problem you cannot solve with horses.
Another grandson, Kublai Khan, founded the Yuan dynasty in twelve seventy-one. By twelve seventy-nine, he had conquered the whole of China.
At its peak, the empire covered roughly twenty-three to twenty-four million square kilometres. That's about the size of the whole of North America.
But it was too big for one ruler. It split into four great khanates: the Golden Horde, the Chagatai Khanate, the Ilkhanate, and Kublai's Yuan dynasty in China.
And across this vast area, trade along the Silk Roads became safer for a time. Merchants, missionaries and travellers like Marco Polo crossed Asia.
Conquest first... then one of the biggest trade networks the world had ever seen.
Within about a century, the khanates weakened. In thirteen sixty-eight, the Yuan dynasty was driven out of China by the Ming.
But the Mongol world changed history. It moved people, ideas and goods across Eurasia... and, many historians believe, it helped diseases like the Black Death spread too.
From a boy abandoned on the steppe... to an empire stretching from Korea to Eastern Europe.
Not bad for a few horses. Next time on Tiny Empires: how a trading company ended up running a country.
Running an empire this size needed more than soldiers.
Ogedei built a capital at Karakorum, in the heart of Mongolia, where envoys and merchants arrived from across Asia and Europe.
Officials and messengers carried a paiza, a metal tablet that worked a bit like a passport. Show it, and the relay stations had to give you fresh horses and supplies.
The khans were generally tolerant of different religions. Buddhists, Christians, Muslims and Taoists could all be found at the Mongol court.

And some of the most powerful people in the empire were women. Sorghaghtani Beki, a Christian princess from the Kerait people, raised four sons. Two became Great Khan, Mongke and Kublai, and a third, Hulagu, ruled Persia.
So... the real boss was Mum.
Pretty much.
In China, Kublai's government ran on paper money, centuries before most of Europe used it.
And a Venetian merchant named Marco Polo later claimed, in a famous book, that he served at Kublai's court for many years. Historians still debate how much of his story is accurate.
